lesson.title: The Skin on the Water: Why Insects Can Walk on Ponds
lesson.summary: Surface tension is the elastic-like pull at a liquid's surface created by hydrogen bonding between water molecules, and it is strong enough to let insects walk on ponds and to help pull water up a tree.
lesson.body:
Water is a bent, polar molecule: oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself more strongly than hydrogen does, leaving the oxygen end slightly negative and each hydrogen end slightly positive. This uneven charge distribution lets one water molecule form a hydrogen bond with a neighboring molecule, and each molecule can do this with several neighbors at once. That constant hydrogen bonding is the same property behind cohesion, water molecules sticking to each other, and adhesion, water sticking to other polar surfaces. Surface tension is simply what cohesion looks like at the boundary between water and air.

Picture a water molecule deep inside a glass of water. It is surrounded on all sides by other water molecules, so the hydrogen bonds pulling on it from every direction cancel out and it feels no net force. A molecule sitting right at the surface is different: it has neighbors beside it and below it, but almost nothing pulling from above, since air molecules barely interact with it. The result is an unbalanced net pull downward and sideways, into the bulk of the liquid. Across the whole surface, this pulls water molecules as tightly together as possible, which is why droplets bead up into spheres rather than spreading flat, a sphere being the shape with the least surface area for a given volume. That taut, elastic-feeling layer at the surface is what we call surface tension.

Water striders, insects in the genus Gerris, exploit this surface film directly. Their legs are covered in thousands of tiny, waxy, hydrophobic hairs that trap air and resist wetting, so the insect's weight spreads over a wide enough area that it dimples the surface without breaking through the hydrogen-bonded film. Push down gently on that dimpled surface and you are essentially pressing on a trampoline made of water molecules holding onto each other. Add a drop of dish soap, which disrupts hydrogen bonding at the surface and lowers surface tension, and the strider sinks, which is exactly how soap-based insect traps work.

Surface tension also shapes the curved meniscus where water meets a narrow glass or plant tube. Inside the microscopic xylem vessels of a tree, water molecules adhere to the polar cellulose walls while also cohering to each other through hydrogen bonds, and the same surface forces that create tension at an open air-water boundary help pull a continuous thread of water upward as it evaporates from pores on the leaves. Without strong cohesion and the surface tension it produces, that unbroken water column would break apart under its own weight long before it reached a tall tree's crown.

This surface film is strong enough to be a habitat in its own right. Mosquito larvae hang from it using hydrophobic breathing tubes, and some spiders and beetles hunt across it, but the same tension only works at small scales; a diving swimmer breaks through it easily because gravity and momentum overwhelm the comparatively weak hydrogen bonds holding the surface together. Surface tension is a useful reminder that a single molecular property, water's polarity and its hydrogen bonding, radiates outward into effects at every size, from one meniscus to an entire pond supporting life on its skin.
